_comment: Practice quizzes for Study With Rameen. History & Geography quizzes are from Rameen's own lecture notes (2059 syllabus). Islamiyat quizzes (2058 syllabus) are drafted from her own exam notes but NOT yet reviewed by her for religious accuracy — do not treat as final until she has checked them. Every question keeps 'topic' and 'question_type' for future flexibility. How to edit: see data/README.md.

questions.question: In which year did Aurangzeb re-impose the Jizya Tax on non-Muslims?
Who defeated the Mughals in 1738–39, looted the treasury, and carried off the Peacock Throne?
The British victories at the Battle of Plassey (1757) and the Battle of Buxar (1764) gave them the riches of which region?
Roughly how long did Aurangzeb's wars against the Marathas in the Deccan last?
What was 'Suttee', the practice that Aurangzeb banned?
options: A Hindu tradition in which a widow was burnt alive with her husband's body

questions.question: Give four reasons for the decline of the Mughal Empire DURING the reign of Aurangzeb.
model_answer: The Maratha / Deccan wars lasted 25 years, drained the treasury and forced higher taxes
Economic decline through extravagance — luxurious palaces and mosques (e.g. the Pearl Mosque)
Intolerance towards non-Muslims — re-imposing the Jizya Tax (1679), causing the Rajputs to revolt
Intolerance towards non-Muslims — destruction of Hindu temples
Intolerance towards non-Muslims — banning of Suttee
Intolerance towards Muslims — the law taxing men who did not keep a set beard length
Failing to educate his sons in the art of ruling (Bahadur Shah I became ruler at 63 with no experience)
questions.marking_note: Any four points earn full marks — extra points are listed so every valid answer is covered.

questions.question: Give four reasons for the decline of the Mughal Empire AFTER the death of Aurangzeb.
model_answer: Succession disputes — there was no law of succession, so sons fought costly wars for the throne
Administrative weakness — the empire was too large; Bengal and Bihar declared independence
Pleasure-seeking, extravagant emperors who ignored administration
Foreign invaders — Nadir Shah (1738–39) and Ahmed Shah Durrani weakened and shrank the empire
British superiority — the Industrial Revolution and victories at Plassey (1757) and Buxar (1764)
questions.marking_note: Any four points earn full marks.

questions.question: What was the Jizya Tax? (4 marks)
model_answer: A tax re-imposed by Aurangzeb in 1679
A protection tax levied on non-Muslims
Charged in return for protecting their temples and places of worship
It was resented by non-Muslims
It led the Rajputs to revolt against the Mughals
questions.marking_note: Any four points earn full marks.

quizzes.subject: history
quizzes.title: The East India Company & British Expansion

questions.question: In which year was the East India Company (EIC) formed, after Queen Elizabeth I granted permission?
Where did the first EIC ship land in India in 1608?
Who led the British to victory at the Battle of Plassey (1757), helped by the treachery of Mir Jafar?
In 1834, which language replaced Persian as the official language of administration in India?
Which traitor helped the British defeat Tipu Sultan and capture Mysore in 1799?
Give three reasons why the East India Company became involved in the Indian subcontinent.
model_answer: India's valuable raw materials — spices, cotton and indigo — were highly demanded in Europe and could be sold at great profit
To oust European rivals (the Dutch and Portuguese) who were already earning large profits, and gain a monopoly over the European markets
The Dutch controlled the spice trade of the East Indies (Indonesia), so India became the EIC's alternate solution
questions.marking_note: Any three points earn full marks.

questions.question: Give four reasons why the British were able to increase their influence in India between 1750 and 1850.
model_answer: The Industrial Revolution gave them technological superiority and modern weaponry
They appointed experienced governors in Madras, Bombay and Calcutta
Military victories at the Battles of Plassey (1757) and Buxar (1764) gave them rich provinces
Indians were not united, so the British easily conquered areas like Sindh and Punjab
Treachery of some Indians — Mir Jafar (Bengal) and Mir Sadiq (Mysore)
A network of roads and railways let them move soldiers quickly and suppress revolts
English replaced Persian as the official language (1834), tightening their political grip
questions.marking_note: Any four points earn full marks.

questions.question: Give three reasons why the British built railways in India during the 19th century.
model_answer: To transport raw materials and to sell their manufactured goods throughout India (more profit)
To suppress revolts — soldiers could travel quickly from one trouble spot to another
To allow people to travel and to bring food to areas affected by famine
questions.marking_note: Any three points earn full marks.

questions.question: Which reformer translated the Holy Quran from Arabic into Persian?
Who launched the Faraizi movement?
Which reformer launched the Jihad movement against the Sikhs of Punjab?
In which battle (1831) was Syed Ahmad Shaheed Barelvi martyred, ending the Jihad movement?
Haji Shariatullah declared India as what, to instil a sense of Jihad among the Muslims of Bengal?
Give three reasons why Shah Waliullah wished to revive Islam in the subcontinent.
model_answer: Muslims had an incomplete knowledge of the Holy Quran — it was in Arabic while common Muslims knew Persian
Sectarianism — the community was divided into groups such as Shias and Sunnis, weakening it
Muslims had adopted corrupt, un-Islamic practices through interaction with non-Muslim communities
questions.marking_note: Any three points earn full marks.

questions.question: Give four reasons why the Jihad movement of Syed Ahmad Shaheed Barelvi failed.
model_answer: His army was untrained (mostly teachers and spiritual leaders) against the well-trained Sikhs under Ranjit Singh
There was a lack of unity among the Muslim forces, who came from different backgrounds
The Pathan tribes refused to accept Muslim leadership they did not control
Taxes imposed on the local population to fund the army angered the locals and lost their support
Limited funds meant a lack of proper weapons and equipment
Internal betrayal by Yar Muhammad Khan (assassination attempts; left the battlefield at Okara)
Traders betrayed the army's route to the Sikhs, enabling the surprise attack
Defeat at the Battle of Balakot (1831), where Syed Ahmad Shaheed Barelvi was martyred
questions.marking_note: Any four points earn full marks — there are eight distinct reasons in the notes.

questions.question: Describe two important contributions of Shah Waliullah to the revival of Islam.
model_answer: He translated the Holy Quran from Arabic into Persian, making its teachings accessible to common people
He inspired his sons (Shah Abdul Qadir and Shah Abdul Aziz) to translate the Quran into Urdu
He wrote an objective account of the four Caliphs, acceptable to both Shias and Sunnis, to unite the Muslims
He wrote 51 books on the Quran, Hadith and Fiqh (e.g. Hujatullah-e-Balighah and Izlat-ul-Akhfah)
He invited Ahmed Shah Abdali, who defeated the Marathas at the Battle of Panipat (1761)
He emphasised social justice — fair pay for labourers and an Islamic mode of trade
questions.marking_note: Any two well-developed contributions earn full marks.

questions.question: Which of the following is a RENEWABLE energy source?
Which major dam is built on the River Jhelum?
In which geological structure is oil trapped, with natural gas above it and water below?
Which is the best quality coal, with the highest carbon content — but not available in Pakistan?
Pakistan's natural gas is produced mainly at which location in Balochistan?
Name the three methods used to mine coal, and state when each is used.
model_answer: Shaft mining — used when coal is deep underground (a vertical shaft is dug)
Adit mining — used when coal is seen on a hillside (a horizontal shaft is dug into the hillside)
Open cast mining — used when coal outcrops on the surface
questions.marking_note: All three methods, each with when it is used.

questions.question: Give four reasons why there is a shortage of electricity in Pakistan.
model_answer: Many power stations are not working to full capacity due to old machinery and poor maintenance
Silt in reservoirs reduces their capacity (less water for HEP) and damages dam machinery
Less rainfall in winter means less water in reservoirs for HEP production
High demand from a growing population
High demand from industrialisation
High demand from an improved standard of living and rural electrification
Theft of electricity and losses on old, poorly maintained transmission lines
questions.marking_note: Any four points earn full marks.

questions.question: Give three reasons why natural gas is widely used for domestic purposes in Pakistan.
model_answer: It is easily available in the main cities through pipelines
It can be transported to remote areas in cylinders
It is cheaper than coal
It is convenient, as firewood is difficult to collect
It is cleaner than coal
questions.marking_note: Any three points earn full marks.

questions.question: How many Fard Rakats are there in the Zuhr prayer?
Who introduced the first (additional) Azan for Friday prayer, to give people further away enough time to travel to the mosque?
How many additional Takbirs are recited during Eid prayer, beyond the standard Takbirs of Ruku and Sajdah?
Which of the following invalidates a Muslim's Wudu?
When is the Khutbah (sermon) delivered during Eid prayer, in contrast to Friday prayer?
options: Before the prayer, same as Friday
There is no Khutbah on Eid

questions.question: Describe how a Muslim should prepare for Friday prayer, and explain what happens once the Khutbah begins.
model_answer: Ghusl (full ritual bath) is Sunnah — Wudu is acceptable if Ghusl is not possible
Using Miswak / brushing teeth and cutting nails before prayer
Wearing one's best, cleanest clothes and applying non-alcoholic perfume
Going early to the mosque, as arriving early earns greater reward
After the Azan, all business and trade must stop (Surah Al-Jumu'ah 62:9)
Once the Khutbah begins, complete silence is obligatory — even reciting Darud aloud is not permitted
Latecomers must sit quietly and listen, not start Nafl prayers
questions.marking_note: Any 4-5 well-explained points earn full marks.

questions.question: List the preconditions (Shurut) that must be met before a Muslim can validly perform Salah.
model_answer: Taharah (ritual purity) — Wudu or Ghusl as required
Clean clothing, free of impurity (Najasah)
A clean place of prayer
Facing the Qibla (the direction of the Ka'bah in Makkah)
Praying within the correct time (Waqt) for that prayer
Making a sincere Niyyah (intention) in the heart
Covering the Awrah — men: navel to knee; women: whole body except face and hands
Having reached puberty and being of sound mind
questions.marking_note: Any 4-5 points earn full marks.

questions.question: Compare Eid ul-Fitr and Eid ul-Adha in terms of date, food eaten before prayer, and the focus of the Khutbah.
model_answer: Eid ul-Fitr is on 1st Shawwal, marking the end of Ramadan; Eid ul-Adha is on 10th Dhul Hijjah, marking the completion of Hajj and Ibrahim's (AS) sacrifice
Before Eid ul-Fitr prayer, Muslims eat an odd number of dates (Sunnah); before Eid ul-Adha prayer, Muslims eat nothing — the first food should come from the Qurbani sacrifice
The Eid ul-Fitr Khutbah focuses on Sadaqah-tul-Fitr (charity for the poor); the Eid ul-Adha Khutbah focuses on Qurbani (sacrifice)
Both are identical in method — 2 Rakats plus 6 additional Takbirs (3 in the first Rakat, 3 in the second)
Eid ul-Adha is usually held slightly earlier than Eid ul-Fitr to allow time for Qurbani
questions.marking_note: Any well-organised comparison covering date, food, and Khutbah focus earns full marks.

questions.question: Which of the following is the SECOND obligation of Hajj?
A pilgrim who performs Hajj al-Qiran (combining Umrah and Hajj in one Ihram) is called a...?
Which type of Hajj is easiest and most commonly performed by pilgrims travelling from overseas (Afaqi)?
Which Tawaf is performed by the pilgrim on arrival at the Holy Ka'bah, on the 8th of Zilhaj?
Which of the following is NOT restricted during the state of Ihram?
Explain how the rituals of Sayee and Rami connect Hajj to the sacrifices of Hazrat Ibrahim's (AS) family.
model_answer: Sayee: Hazrat Hajra (AS) ran seven times between Safa and Marwa searching for water for her infant son Hazrat Ismail (AS) — pilgrims re-enact this with a brisk walk between the two mounts
The fountain of Zamzam appeared when Hazrat Ismail (AS) scraped his heels on the ground — pilgrims drink Zamzam water, without which Tawaf is not considered complete
Rami: Hazrat Ibrahim (AS) was misled by Satan three times on his way to sacrifice his son and stoned the devil three times in response — pilgrims re-enact this by stoning the Jamarat
Both rituals are direct re-enactments of the obedience and sacrifice of Hazrat Ibrahim's (AS) family
questions.marking_note: Explaining both Sayee and Rami with their belief basis earns full marks.

questions.question: Describe the three types of Hajj a pilgrim may perform.
model_answer: Hajj al-Tamattu (Interrupted): Ihram for Umrah is entered first, removed after Umrah is completed, then put on again on the 8th of Zilhaj for Hajj — the easiest and most common type, usually chosen by Afaqi (overseas) pilgrims, involving two separate intentions

Hajj al-Qiran (Combined): Ihram for Umrah and Hajj is entered at the same time and not removed until the 10th of Zilhaj — the pilgrim is called a Qarin; those who live in Makkah cannot perform this type
Hajj al-Ifrad (Single): Ihram is entered for Hajj only, with no Umrah performed beforehand — the pilgrim is called a Mufrid
questions.marking_note: All three types, each with their key distinguishing feature, earn full marks.

questions.question: Explain two ways in which Hajj promotes unity and equality within the Muslim community.
model_answer: All pilgrims wear the same simple Ihram regardless of colour, caste or creed — this removes signs of distinction and promotes equality
Pilgrims from all over the world meet, share news, and discuss issues facing the Ummah — this promotes universal brotherhood
All pilgrims perform the same rituals at the same time and place (e.g. staying in Mina, Rami, sacrifice), reminding them that the Ummah must remain united under one God
Around 2 million Muslims perform Hajj every year, showing the Ummah is strong and secure in its large numbers
questions.marking_note: Any two well-developed points with a 'Thus' style conclusion earn full marks.

questions.question: What is the standard Zakat rate charged on annual savings/cash above the Nisab?
According to Surah At-Taubah 9:60, which of the following is NOT one of the eight recipients of Zakat?
Why can a Muslim not give Zakat to his own wife?
options: Because her maintenance (Nafaqah) is already his financial responsibility

questions.question: In which year after the Hijrah did Zakat become obligatory on all adult wealthy Muslims?
According to Surah At-Taubah 9:34-35, how will those who hoard wealth and withhold Zakat be punished?
options: Their wealth will be confiscated by the state
They will be branded with their own hoarded wealth in the Fire of Hell
They will be forgotten by history

questions.question: Name and briefly explain four of the eight categories of people who may receive Zakat.
model_answer: Poor (Fuqara) — those whose funds are below the Nisab and cannot meet their basic needs
Needy (Masakeen) — those who are helpless and in miserable circumstances, may have some income but it is insufficient
Collectors (Amileen-e-Zakat) — officials appointed by the Islamic government to collect and administer Zakat, paid from Zakat funds even if wealthy
Reconciliation of Hearts (Mu'allafatul-Quloob) — newly converted Muslims whose support benefits the Islamic cause
Freeing of Slaves (Fi-Riqab) — historically freeing slaves; today extended to those unjustly imprisoned or in bonded labour
Debtors (Gharimeen) — those indebted and unable to repay on their own
In the Way of Allah (Fee Sabeelillah) — efforts for justice and the propagation of Islam, including schools, hospitals and mosques
Wayfarers (Ibn-As-Sabeel) — travellers stranded in a foreign land needing assistance, even if wealthy at home
questions.marking_note: Any 4 categories, each correctly named and explained, earn full marks.

questions.question: Give three examples of people who cannot receive Zakat, and explain why in each case.
model_answer: Non-Muslims — Zakat is a specifically Islamic obligation and must stay within the Muslim community (Sadaqah, not Zakat, may be given to them)
The wealthy — anyone above the Nisab threshold is not entitled to receive Zakat, since its purpose is to help those in genuine need
A wife — a husband's Nafaqah (maintenance) obligation to her already covers this, so Zakat cannot substitute it
Children and grandchildren — a Muslim is already financially responsible for his dependants
Parents and grandparents — Islam already requires a Muslim to support needy parents
Descendants of the Holy Prophet (pbuh) — the Banu Hashim are prohibited from receiving Zakat as a matter of honour
questions.marking_note: Any three examples with a reason each earn full marks.

questions.question: Explain the individual and social importance of Zakat for Muslims today.
model_answer: Individual: Zakat purifies the remainder of one's wealth — the word 'Zakat' itself means purification (Surah At-Tawbah 9:103)
Individual: it is an act of obedience to Allah that strengthens faith (Iman) and God-consciousness (Taqwa), and protects from the punishment described in Surah At-Taubah 9:34-35
Social: Zakat directly transfers wealth from rich to poor, reducing poverty and creating a more equitable society
Social: it keeps wealth in circulation rather than hoarded, stimulating the economy
Social: it strengthens the unity of the Ummah, as the rich fulfil their duty of care toward the poor
Social: Fee Sabeelillah funds schools, hospitals and mosques, strengthening Islamic institutions
questions.marking_note: Covering both individual AND social importance, with at least one point each, earns full marks.

questions.question: What is the pre-dawn meal eaten by Muslims before beginning the fast called?
Laylat-ul-Qadr (the Night of Power) falls within which part of Ramadan?
What is the Kaffarah (expiation) for deliberately breaking a fast without a valid excuse (aside from freeing a slave)?
options: Fasting 60 consecutive days OR feeding 60 poor people
Paying a fine equal to one month's income
Fasting for the rest of Ramadan only
There is no Kaffarah, only Qaza

questions.question: Which of these people is permanently exempted from fasting and pays Fidyah instead, with no Qaza required?
options: A woman who has just given birth

questions.question: How many Rakats of Tarawih prayer are offered, at minimum, each night of Ramadan?
Describe what a fasting Muslim must abstain from during Ramadan, from dawn until sunset.
model_answer: Physical abstentions: eating and drinking (including water), smoking, marital relations, and any deliberate act that breaks the fast
Moral/spiritual abstentions: lying, cheating, backbiting and abusing others
Arguing, fighting and quarrelling; indecent speech and actions; wasting time in idle activities
Hadith: 'If a person does not avoid false talk and false conduct during the fast, then Allah does not need him to abstain from food and drink' (Sahih al-Bukhari)
Normal life must continue — no special workplace concessions, and daily responsibilities and the five daily prayers continue as normal
questions.marking_note: Must include BOTH physical and moral abstentions for full marks.

questions.question: Describe the difference between temporary and permanent exemptions from fasting, giving an example of each.
model_answer: Temporary exemptions must make up the missed fasts later (Qaza) once able — examples: the sick, travellers, pregnant and breastfeeding mothers, and women during menstruation or Nifas
Permanent exemptions are never required to make up the fasts — instead, some must pay Fidyah (feeding a poor person for each missed day) — examples: the elderly and the chronically ill
Children and the insane are permanently excused with no Qaza or Fidyah required, since they are not held accountable for acts of worship
Note: women during menstruation ARE required to make up fasts later, unlike other permanent exemptions
questions.marking_note: Clear distinction between temporary (Qaza) and permanent (Fidyah/none), with named examples, earns full marks.

questions.question: Explain the individual and communal importance of fasting for Muslims.
model_answer: Individual: fasting builds Taqwa (God-consciousness) and self-control — the Qur'an says it is prescribed 'so that you may learn self-restraint' (2:183)
Individual: the Prophet (pbuh) said fasting is 'a shield by which a servant protects himself from the Fire', and there is a gate of Paradise, Rayyan, only for those who fast
Communal: experiencing hunger builds empathy for the poor and breaks down class barriers, since rich and poor share the same experience
Communal: Muslims worldwide fast simultaneously, creating a profound sense of global unity within the Ummah
Communal: Sadaqah-tul-Fitr at the end of Ramadan ensures even the poorest Muslims can celebrate Eid with dignity
questions.marking_note: Covering both individual AND communal importance earns full marks.

questions.question: What are angels created from, according to Islamic belief?
Which angel will blow the trumpet (Sur) to signal the end of time and, later, the resurrection of the dead?
Which two angels question the deceased in their grave about their faith, Lord, and Prophet?
What is the key difference between angels and humans regarding free will?
options: Angels have free will but humans do not
Neither angels nor humans have free will
Angels have no free will and can only obey Allah, while humans can choose good or evil

questions.question: Which pre-Islamic belief about angels does Islam explicitly reject?
options: That angels were the daughters of Allah

questions.question: Name and describe the duties of four named angels in Islam.
model_answer: Jibrael (AS) — chief of all angels; brought revelation to the Prophets and conducted the Holy Prophet (pbuh) on the Night of Mi'raj
Israfil (AS) — will blow the trumpet (Sur) to end the world, then blow it again to resurrect the dead for Judgement
Izrael (AS) (Malak-ul-Maut) — the Angel of Death, responsible for collecting the souls of all living beings
Mikael (AS) — responsible for celestial bodies, food, rain and natural provisions
Kiram-un-Katibeen — two angels assigned to every human, recording good deeds (right) and bad deeds (left)
Munkir and Nakir — question the deceased in the grave about their faith, Lord and Prophet
Malik — keeper of Hellfire (Jahannam); Rizwan — keeper of Paradise (Jannah)
Hamalat-ul-Arsh — the angels who bear the Throne of Allah
questions.marking_note: Any four named angels with a correct duty each earn full marks.

questions.question: Compare angels and humans in terms of free will, accountability and rank before Allah.
model_answer: Free will: angels have none and can only obey Allah; humans were given free will and can choose between good and evil
Accountability: angels are not held accountable on the Day of Judgement, since they have no choice; humans are fully accountable for their choices

Rank before Allah: despite their power, angels are inferior in rank to humans — they prostrated before Hazrat Adam (AS) on Allah's orders, showing that Allah made man His Khalifah (vicegerent) on earth
Only Iblis (from the Jinn, not an angel) refused to prostrate, since Jinn — unlike angels — have free will
questions.marking_note: Covering all three points of comparison (free will, accountability, rank) earns full marks.

questions.question: Explain why belief in Angels is significant for a Muslim's daily life.
model_answer: Belief in angels completes Iman (faith) — it is explicitly listed in Iman-e-Mufassal as the second Article of Faith, without which faith is incomplete
Knowing that Kiram-un-Katibeen record every deed motivates a Muslim to avoid sin even in private, creating constant moral accountability
Belief in Izrael (AS), the Angel of Death, reminds the Muslim that death can come at any moment, encouraging sincere and timely repentance
Believing that Jibrael (AS) brought the Qur'an to the Prophet (pbuh) validates the entire chain of revelation and prophecy
Belief in Malik and Rizwan creates a healthy balance of fear of punishment and hope for reward
questions.marking_note: Any two well-developed points earn AO2-level marks; more points needed for a fuller AO1 answer.
